chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ṣafwān, from Ibn Bukayr, from ʿUbayd ibn Zurārah, who said:
I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about flour: may wudu be done with it? He said: There is no harm in using it for washing and benefiting from it.

So the correct understanding of his statement, 'There is no harm in using it for washing,' is that he only meant by it the washing that is beautification and rubbing the body with it, not the wudu for salat (prayer). And that which clarifies this is what...

key_terms.التَّحْسِينُ: beautification or grooming, meaning non-ritual bodily cleansing
key_terms.الدَّقِيقِ: flour, the substance being asked about for ritual use
key_terms.الْوُضُوءَ: washing; here distinguished between general cleansing and ritual wudu (ablution)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: there is no harm; an expression of permissibility in a qualified sense
key_terms.لِلصَّلَاةِ: for salat (prayer), indicating the specific ritual context
key_terms.يُتَوَضَّأُ: to perform washing; here clarified as not meaning the ritual wudu for salat (prayer)

ai.seo_question: Can flour be used for wudu (ablution) or tayammum in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the use of flour in the context of ritual purity. The apparent wording is clarified to mean ordinary washing or bodily cleansing, not the wudu (ablution) required for salat (prayer), which supports the ruling that flour is not valid for tayammum or ritual wudu.
